table_reddening.source: The compiled table (sn2006aj.csv) carries no extinction column; its `source` column holds ADS bibliography codes plus one archive name (CfA Supernova Archive), which says where the numbers came from but not what was done to them. What the *literature* says about this line of sight is on the record, though: Sollerman et al. 2006, A&A 454, 503, DOI 10.1051/0004-6361:20065226, section 3 give "the Galactic extinction of E(B-V)=0.14" from the Schlegel maps, argue the host term is low from the host SED and the Balmer decrement, and then "adopt a total extinction of E(B-V) = 0.14 mag" -- i.e. at that level the Galactic and the adopted total figure coincide, so the host term they assume is ~0.  That is a statement about the sky, not about this table's provenance, so the declaration stays `unknown`: the compilation neither confirms nor denies that it removed anything.  docs/VALIDATION.md section B records the one thing the comparison does constrain: read as it stands, the table's brightest V row sits 0.045 mag from the published peak, whereas a table that had already been de-reddened by A_V = 3.1 x 0.14 would sit 0.389 mag from it.  The evidence therefore says this table has *not* had the dust taken off it.  That is an inference from a magnitude comparison, not a provenance statement, so it is kept labelled as one and not promoted into the declaration above.

unfold.correction_model: per-epoch, penalised second difference in time
unfold.gain_definition: dM_band / d(log10 L_nu at the node), finite difference on the assembled surface; -2.5 is the delta-band limit

band_admission.rule: one departure at a time, worst excess first, undone when it pushed a band that was inside the cap outside it

template.label: SN 2006aj / GRB 060218 (type Ic-BL associated with a low-luminosity GRB)
template.z_source:
Sollerman et al. 2006, A&A 454, 503, DOI 10.1051/0004-6361:20065226, section 2: "From the narrow emission lines from the host galaxy we derive a redshift of z = 0.0331 +- 0.0007."  Adopted here because it is the value the same paper's distance and absolute magnitudes were derived with, which is what docs/VALIDATION.md section A re-derives.  v1 carried 0.033 in its module and 0.0343 in the notebook that consumed it, both without a stated source; 0.033 agrees with the published value to the 2 decimals it quotes, 0.0343 does not. Independent cross-check: Mirabal et al. 2006, ApJ 643, L99, DOI 10.1086/505177, "The weighted mean heliocentric redshift derived from the emission lines is z = 0.03345 +- 0.00006" -- 0.5 sigma of the adopted value, which is where a redshift enters the error budget at this distance: 0.00035 in z is 1.08 % in d_L, i.e. 0.023 mag.
What that +-0.0007 actually is, because it is not a measurement precision and reading it as one would be the mistake this repository exists to prevent. Sect. 3.2 of the same paper: "We derived the redshift by measuring the positions of the [O II] line, the [O III] lines as well as Halpha and Hbeta at all 4 epochs, and conclude z = 0.0331 +- 0.0007." Its own Table 1 gives those positions: [O II] 3853.42 A -> z = 0.0338, and Hbeta, [O III] 4958.91, [O III] 5006.84 and Halpha -> 0.0328. So the quoted +-0.0007 spans the disagreement between the [O II] and the Balmer lines: it measures how well the narrow lines pin the *systemic* velocity of the star-forming gas, and is 1.5x the sample scatter of those five values. It is not a centroid error either -- sect. 2.2 gives 3 A per pixel, so a line centroid is good to ~0.1 pixel = 0.3 A = 1.4e-4 in z, five times tighter than 0.0007, and Mirabal+2006 measured the same lines to +-0.00006. 0.0007 in z is 210 km/s, which is why it reads like a velocity; it is not one. A line-of-sight scatter about the systemic velocity and the galaxy's bulk motion relative to the CMB are separate unknowns -- a bulk motion shifts every line equally, so it cannot appear in the scatter among them -- and the bulk motion is handled where it belongs, by the CMB frame declared above, where it comes to 175.3 km/s. The error is recorded here and deliberately *not* folded into `Distance.distance_error_mag`: the 350 km/s term there is already a line-of-sight velocity dispersion, so adding 210 km/s of the same class of quantity counts one unknown twice, raising this template's distance error from 0.0780 to 0.0893 mag for no new information. docs/VERIFICATION.md sect. 13 works the comparison for all four templates.

distance.source: z = 0.0331 is above the peculiar-velocity guard (0.02), so a cosmological luminosity distance is defensible; the default cosmology is used and named in every result's provenance block, and it is `constants.DEFAULT_COSMOLOGY_NAME` that the build reads.  Note that this is *not* the distance the comparison above uses: Sollerman et al. 2006 state "a cosmology where H_0 = 70 km/s/Mpc, Omega_Lambda = 0.7 and Omega_m = 0.3, this corresponds to a luminosity distance of 145.4 Mpc", so docs/VALIDATION.md section A passes that paper's own cosmology as an explicit `Distance` instead of inheriting this default.  The two differ by 0.073 mag of distance modulus, which is the price of an unstated H0 and the reason a distance never travels without its provenance.

citations:
redshift, distance and published peak/absolute magnitudes (comparison anchors
       only, never photometry): Sollerman et al. 2006, A&A 454, 503,
       DOI 10.1051/0004-6361:20065226; redshift cross-checked against Mirabal et al.
       2006, ApJ 643, L99, DOI 10.1086/505177
table source column: 2014Ap&SS.354...89B (as compiled in the AJST catalogue)

K-correction formalism: Hogg, Baldry, Blanton & Eisenstein 2002, "The K
       correction", arXiv:astro-ph/0210394.  Never refereed, so it has no journal ref
       and no DOI: cite the arXiv id. Equations used: 2 (m_R = M_Q + DM + K_QR),
       3 (DM = 5 log10(D_L/10 pc)), 6 (L_nu = 4 pi D_L^2 f_nu / (1+z))
